| Nights failed | Treatment |
|---|---|
| One | Watched |
| Two | Worked during the day |
| **Three consecutive** | **No longer an operational matter — a formal incident record is opened** |

You are at the third rung. The unagreed days now span a statement cycle, and that is the fact that makes this formal.

**The job keeps running on its schedule while the incident is open.** Do not pause, disable, or suspend it. Closure depends on the scheduled run itself passing (see §7), so a disabled control cannot produce the evidence that closes the record.

---

## 2. Open the record

Open an **IN-28 incident record**. This is mandatory at the third consecutive failed night; it is not a judgment call. ([Settlement Recon Job Runbook](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_37f4f072-3302-4571-9985-1288bb56cfa7))

The runbook's own scope ends at opening the record honestly — everything after opening is governed by the standards below, not by the job's operators. In particular, **you do not choose the severity.**

Record on opening, at minimum:
- The control: nightly settlement-recon.
- The three nights in question, by date.
- The days now unagreed as a result.
- The severity band, assigned per §3.

---

## 3. Severity

Severity is assigned when the record is opened and belongs to the standard, not to the team that opened it. ([Incident Severity Standard](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_6f594637-e078-4f3d-854c-a9768b176d4d))

**This incident is band SB-8.** The standard states plainly: a reconciliation or settlement control failing across a statement cycle is band SB-8. Three consecutive failed settlement-recon nights is exactly that case — the runbook opens the record precisely because the unagreed days span a statement cycle.

Do not assign a lighter band. The lighter bands cover single-night failures and non-control degradations; they notify the owning team only and do not escalate unattended. Neither description fits this situation.

Band SB-8 carries three consequences, all of which follow automatically:
1. It notifies the owning team and the platform group's shift lead **at opening** (§4).
2. It escalates along the **garnet route** (§5).
3. It may carry a regulatory notification obligation that is not the engineering organization's to schedule (§6).

---

## 4. Who has to be told, at opening

Band SB-8 notifies, at the moment the record is opened:

- **The owning team** of the settlement-recon control.
- **The platform group's shift lead.**

The shift lead is also the first rung of the garnet escalation route (§5), so this notification is both an information notice and the start of the escalation clock.

The opening notice content is governed by the communications standard — see §8. Send the opening notice at opening; do not defer it while you investigate.

> The available material names the owning team only as "the owning team" and does not identify which team owns settlement-recon, nor does it give contact channels or named individuals for any role. See **Open items**.

---

## 5. Escalation: the garnet route and its clocks

### 5.1 The ladder

A route is an ordered ladder of roles. An escalation climbs it **one rung at a time** and **never skips a rung that has acknowledged.** ([Escalation Roster](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_50eaba66-935e-47d3-adae-3497098d9997))

The garnet route, in order:

| Rung | Role | Hold clock |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Platform shift lead | **23 minutes** |
| 2 | Duty manager | **34 minutes** |
| 3 | Head of platform operations | **Holds until answered** |

The clocks are the settlement family of routes' clocks, recorded in the [Acknowledgment Clock Table](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_709ae357-3908-4c5e-aeea-7c0ca8c927ea). The final rung holds until answered because there is nowhere further to climb — there is no fourth rung and no timeout that ends the climb.

The clocks belong to the clock table, not to the roster, so a clock change never edits a route. If you are reading a cached copy of either page, read the clock table for the clocks and the roster for the ladder.

### 5.2 What happens when nobody responds — rule AC-15

Rule AC-15 governs expiry ([Acknowledgment Clock Table](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_709ae357-3908-4c5e-aeea-7c0ca8c927ea)):

- **A clock that runs out without an acknowledgment advances the call to the next rung on its own.** You do not have to push it, and you must not hold it back.
- **The missed rung is recorded as missed, not re-tried.** Do not re-page a rung whose clock expired, and do not treat a late acknowledgment as restarting that rung. Write "missed" against it in the record.
- **Acknowledging stops the climb at that rung.** Once the shift lead acknowledges, the call does not proceed to the duty manager on the clock.
- **Declining passes it upward immediately, without waiting out the clock.** A decline at rung 1 sends it to the duty manager now, not in 23 minutes.

### 5.3 The unattended sequence, concretely

If nobody responds at any point, the sequence from the opening notification is:

- **T+0** — Record opened; platform shift lead notified (rung 1). 23-minute clock starts.
- **T+23 min** — No acknowledgment. Rung 1 recorded as missed. Call advances to the duty manager (rung 2). 34-minute clock starts.
- **T+57 min** — No acknowledgment. Rung 2 recorded as missed. Call advances to the head of platform operations (rung 3).
- **After T+57 min** — Rung 3 holds until answered. There is no further advance and no expiry. The call stays live at the head of platform operations until it is answered.

Because band SB-8 notifies the shift lead at opening and the garnet route's first rung *is* the shift lead, treat the opening notification as the start of the rung-1 clock. (The material does not restate this in so many words; see **Open items**.)

### 5.4 If an escalation is already in flight

An escalation in flight finishes on the roster it started on. If the roster is edited mid-incident, your climb continues on the version you started under. Routes change only by agreement between the owning teams and the platform group, and only after the change is agreed in writing.

---

## 6. The regulatory obligation — check this early

Bands touching settlement controls carry one more obligation that is **not the engineering organization's to schedule**. When the failure falls inside a statutory filing window, notification follows the regulatory filing calendar maintained by the compliance office. ([Incident Severity Standard](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_6f594637-e078-4f3d-854c-a9768b176d4d))

**Do this as a first-hour action, not at closure.** The timing rule is unforgiving:

- The compliance office maintains the calendar of statutory filing windows. Windows are published a year ahead; each names its filing, the lodgment date, and the list of in-scope arrangements the filing draws on. ([Regulatory Filing Calendar](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_3e479c9f-3eb8-4c99-8bfa-607aab21bc02))
- Where anything on the in-scope list was interrupted while a filing was being prepared, **form RN-26** is lodged with the filing **before the window closes**, stating what was interrupted, the days affected, and the basis on which the filed figures stand.
- **The office can only lodge what it has been told while the window is open.** Word that arrives after lodgment becomes a correction, which the regulators treat differently.

Concrete steps:

1. Determine whether the three failed nights fall inside an open statutory filing window, and whether settlement-recon (or the settlement records it agrees) appears on that window's in-scope list.
2. If either question is unclear, put it to the compliance office **in writing**. The office confirms scope questions in writing within a working day.
3. If it is in scope and a window is open, tell the compliance office now, so RN-26 can be lodged before the window closes. Supply: what was interrupted, the days affected, and what you can say about the basis on which the figures stand.
4. Record in the incident what you asked, when, and what the office answered.

Note also that during a window the office's attention belongs to the filing, not to new requests — so a late-arriving request may not be absorbed. This is another reason to check on day one.

> The filing calendar's actual window dates and in-scope lists are not available in the material read here, so this document cannot tell you whether 2026-08-10 sits inside a window. That determination must come from the compliance office. See **Open items**.

---

## 7. What is communicated while the incident is open

Cadence **UC-11** applies to control-failure incidents, which this is. ([Incident Communications Standard](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_c4d09ec2-0c36-488f-94f6-df16bf92b1f4))

### 7.1 The opening notice

The opening notice must name:
- **The affected control** — the nightly settlement-recon job.
- **The days in question** — the three failed nights and the days left unagreed.
- **When the next update will arrive.**

The third element is the important one: **an open incident communicates on the cadence its opening notice declared, and the cadence is a promise.** You choose and state the cadence in the opening notice; from that moment it binds you.

### 7.2 Every update thereafter

- Each update either **reports progress** or **re-promises the next time honestly**. "Nothing to report, next update at HH:MM" is a valid update. Silence is not.
- **Missing an update is itself reportable.** Treat a missed update as a reportable failure in its own right, not as a minor slip.
- **Updates go to the same audience as the opening notice. Narrowing the audience mid-incident is not permitted, however quiet the update.** Do not drop recipients because an update is uneventful, and do not move the conversation to a smaller channel.

### 7.3 The closing notice

The closing notice is part of the standard too. It goes to **the full audience** and **names the evidence the closure rests on** — that is, the CE-2 record described in §8.

---

## 8. What has to be true before it can be closed

**A control-failure incident closes on evidence, not on silence.** ([Closure Evidence Standard](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_2241ab18-81be-445a-b823-75ddcf24d941))

Closure requires a **CE-2 evidence record**. All of the following must hold:

1. **The control passes on its own schedule.** The evidence must come from the scheduled run itself.
2. **Unassisted.** A manually forced pass does not qualify.
3. **The previously unagreed days are brought current.** A clean pass on tonight's data alone is not enough — the days that were left unagreed must be agreed.

Two explicit disqualifiers, stated in the standard:

- **A manually forced pass does not qualify.** If you push the job through by hand to get a green result, that result cannot close the incident.
- **A quiet night with the control disabled qualifies even less.** Absence of failure is not evidence of a pass.

**The CE-2 record is attached to the incident before the closing notice goes out.** Order matters: attach the evidence, then send the closing notice naming it (§7.3).

### 8.1 Repairing the unagreed nights

The runbook's normal repair path is that a failed pass is re-attempted the following night after the upstream statements refresh. Where a re-run is used to repair a bad night, procedure **RP-22** governs it ([Feed Re-run Procedure](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_01fc3369-f4ff-482b-acb2-65f491e0e021)):

- A re-run repairs a bad night **by replacing it, never by appending to it.** Affected write-date partitions are replaced whole, under the feed's own prefix.
- **The original write date stays the partition's identity.** A re-run performed days later still lands under the night it repairs, so consumers re-reading the partition see the corrected records where the bad ones were. A re-run that would change a partition's write date is not a re-run — it is a new feed writing into an old feed's zone, and the layout forbids it.
- **Re-runs happen after the upstream collectors have drained for the affected window.** Re-running ahead of the upstream repair reproduces the bad night.

Note the interaction with CE-2: repairing partitions may be necessary to bring the unagreed days current, but the passing result that closes the incident must still come from the scheduled, unassisted run. A repair does not substitute for that pass.

> RP-22 is written for a nightly *feed's* bad night; the settlement-recon runbook does not itself point at it. Confirm applicability before relying on it here. See **Open items**.

---

## 9. The record it has to leave behind

Closure is not the end. **Once closed, the incident owes one more artifact: the review record.** It is due on the review standard's own clock, **not at closure time** — do not treat closing the incident as discharging it.

### 9.1 PM-6 review record

Every closed control-failure incident files a **PM-6 review record** ([Review Record Standard](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_5b8884ab-b5dc-41d4-b87c-f8dd772eee1d)). It carries:

1. **A timeline of the nights in question.**
2. **The originating conditions as they are actually understood** — not a tidied-up or speculative account.
3. **The corrections that will be made, with a named owner for each.**
4. **The review meeting's outcome.**

Rules attached to it:

- **Owned corrections are tracked to completion.** Filing the record does not close the corrections.
- **A record whose corrections have no owner is returned to the incident's owner rather than filed.** Every correction needs a name against it before the record will be accepted.

### 9.2 Where it lives

The record is filed **against the incident** and **referenced from the control's own operating notes** — that is, from the Settlement Recon Job Runbook — so the next operator to meet the same failure finds what the last one learned. Both placements are required; filing against the incident alone leaves the runbook silent.

### 9.3 The people side — do this before filing

**Hours spent on the nights in question are entered under the worked-hours ledger practice *before* the review record is filed**, because the workforce office's ledger closes on its own rhythm whether or not the review is done.

Per the [Worked Hours Ledger Practice](mcp:knowledge_page:kp_27b913c8-a1d4-4f0d-a057-ca16f88c5352):

- Ordinary working days flow into the ledger from badge records without anyone's attention. **Hours worked outside the working day are different**: they are entered **by hand**, under code **TL-19**, with **the date** and **a one-line purpose**.
- The deadline is **before the payroll cutoff of the following week**.
- **An unentered line lapses.** The ledger closes with payroll, and a late claim reopens nothing.
- Entered TL-19 hours accrue toward time off in lieu at the rate the employment terms set; the balance is visible beside leave in the workforce portal.
- A correction to a closed period is a payroll correction: applied by the payroll administrators on the following run, adjusting pay, never the closed ledger itself. Questions about a closed period go to the workforce office **in writing** and are answered against the ledger as it closed.

For a three-night settlement incident this matters directly: night work on the failed nights and on the incident is out-of-working-day time and will not appear on its own. Enter it by hand, per night, before the following week's payroll cutoff.

---

## 10. On-shift checklist

**At opening (now):**

- [ ] Confirm three consecutive failed nights and record the dates.
- [ ] Open the IN-28 incident record.
- [ ] Assign severity **SB-8** (per standard, not by judgment).
- [ ] Notify the owning team and the platform group's shift lead.
- [ ] Send the opening notice naming: the control, the days in question, and when the next update will arrive.
- [ ] Note the rung-1 (23-minute) clock start time in the record.
- [ ] Confirm the job remains enabled and on schedule.
- [ ] Ask the compliance office, in writing, whether the failure falls inside an open statutory filing window and whether the control is on the in-scope list.

**On the escalation clocks (unattended):**

- [ ] T+23 min, no ack → record rung 1 missed; call advances to duty manager; 34-minute clock starts.
- [ ] T+57 min, no ack → record rung 2 missed; call advances to head of platform operations; holds until answered.
- [ ] Any acknowledgment → climb stops at that rung; record it.
- [ ] Any decline → pass upward immediately; do not wait out the clock.

**While open:**

- [ ] Send every update on the promised cadence, to the full opening audience, unnarrowed.
- [ ] Each update reports progress or honestly re-promises the next time.
- [ ] If a filing window is open and in scope, get the RN-26 facts to the compliance office before the window closes.
- [ ] If repairing nights by re-run: upstream drained first; partitions replaced whole; original write dates preserved.

**To close:**

- [ ] Scheduled run passes, unassisted, with the previously unagreed days brought current.
- [ ] CE-2 evidence record produced from that scheduled run.
- [ ] CE-2 attached to the incident.
- [ ] Closing notice sent to the full audience, naming the evidence.

**After closing:**

- [ ] TL-19 hours entered by hand for the nights in question, with date and one-line purpose, before next week's payroll cutoff.
- [ ] PM-6 review record drafted: timeline, originating conditions as actually understood, corrections each with a named owner, review meeting outcome.
- [ ] PM-6 filed against the incident.
- [ ] PM-6 referenced from the Settlement Recon Job Runbook.
- [ ] Owned corrections tracked to completion.

---

## Open items

The following are things this document needs and the available material does not supply. Each must be resolved by the on-shift engineer or the incident owner before the corresponding step can be executed as written.

1. **The identity of the owning team.** Band SB-8 notifies "the owning team," and the settlement-recon runbook does not name which team owns the job. Unlike the other pipelines recorded here (which name a duty group in their runbooks), the settlement-recon runbook is silent on ownership. This must be established before the opening notification in §4 can be sent.

2. **Contact channels and named individuals for every role.** The escalation roster gives roles — platform shift lead, duty manager, head of platform operations — but no names, rotas, or paging channels. The roster states that severity decides the route and the roster decides the names, but the names themselves are not in the material read here.

3. **The full notification audience for the opening notice.** The communications standard forbids narrowing the audience mid-incident but does not enumerate who that audience is beyond the two parties the severity standard names at opening. Whether the audience is exactly those two, or wider, is undetermined.

4. **The update interval.** UC-11 makes the cadence a promise but sets no default interval — the cadence is whatever the opening notice declares. No recommended or minimum interval for SB-8 is recorded, so the on-shift engineer must choose one and will be held to it.

5. **Whether the escalation clock starts at the opening notification.** The severity standard notifies the shift lead at opening and the garnet route begins at the shift lead; this document reads the two as the same event, starting the 23-minute clock at opening. The material does not state this explicitly, and it does not say what else, if anything, initiates the climb.

6. **Whether the three nights fall inside a statutory filing window, and whether settlement-recon is on the in-scope list.** The filing calendar's window dates, filings, and in-scope arrangements are maintained by the compliance office and are not in the material read here. This must be confirmed with that office in writing; the office answers scope questions within a working day.

7. **Whether RP-22 applies to settlement-recon.** The Feed Re-run Procedure governs a nightly *feed's* bad night. The settlement-recon runbook describes re-attempt on the following night but does not cite RP-22. Whether settlement-recon partitions are repaired under RP-22 is unconfirmed.

8. **The PM-6 due date.** The closure evidence standard says the review record is due "on the standard's own clock rather than at closure time," but the review record standard does not state what that clock is. The deadline for filing PM-6 is therefore undetermined.

9. **The review meeting itself.** PM-6 records "the review meeting's outcome," but who convenes it, who attends, and when it is held are not specified.

10. **Where the IN-28 record is opened.** No incident tracker, system, or record location is named in the material. The mechanics of opening the record must come from local knowledge.

11. **The definition of "statement cycle" and of a "night."** The runbook's threshold rests on the unagreed days spanning a statement cycle, but the cycle's length, and the timezone and cutoff that define a failed night, are not recorded.

12. **The payroll cutoff date.** TL-19 hours are due before "the payroll cutoff of the following week"; the actual cutoff day and time are held by the workforce office and are not stated here.

# invoice-adjustments — Feed Onboarding Document

**Status:** onboarding draft for a new nightly feed
**Basis:** operated exactly like the `parcel-events` feed
**Date:** 2026-08-10

---

## 1. Scope and how to read this document

`invoice-adjustments` is a new nightly feed to be stood up and operated exactly as the `parcel-events` feed is operated.

The Parcel Events Feed Runbook is deliberately thin: it states that `parcel-events` is *"the model other nightly feeds are stood up from, and everything that makes it operable lives in the standards it follows rather than in this page."* The runbook itself carries only two things of its own — what the feed writes and its dependency on upstream collectors draining — and then points at six standards:

| Concern | Governing standard | Rule identifier |
|---|---|---|
| Feed and output naming | Feed Naming Standard | pattern **FN-13** |
| Where output lands, how the area is organized | Landing Zone Layout | layout **LZ-14** |
| Storage registration and output lifetime | Storage Tier Register | tier **ST-16** |
| Expected landing time and lateness | Delivery Expectation Standard | table **LH-18** |
| Repair after a bad night | Feed Re-run Procedure | procedure **RP-22** |
| Copies leaving the platform | Off-platform Copy Policy | approval **EG-24** |

Operating `invoice-adjustments` "exactly like `parcel-events`" therefore means registering it under these same six standards. This document works through each in turn, and follows each standard's onward references (storage capacity, consumer notice, records filing, data-sharing instruments) to the point where the obligation leaves the feed team's hands.

Nothing about `invoice-adjustments` itself is recorded on the platform today — searches for the feed by name return no runbook, no catalog entry, and no prior operating notes. Everything below is the standard as it applies to a new feed of this kind; anything that must be a *specific* value for this feed (an hour, an owner, an upstream) is called out where it arises and collected in **Open items**.

---

## 2. Naming

### 2.1 The feed name

Feed names follow **pattern FN-13**: the subject first, then the grain of the records, joined with a dash. `parcel-events` is the standard's own worked example — subject `parcel`, grain `events`.

`invoice-adjustments` is well-formed under FN-13 on the same reading: subject `invoice`, grain `adjustments`. The name may be used as given.

The standard's stated reason matters operationally: *a feed's name is its contract with everyone who schedules against it.* Consumers schedule against the name, so the name is not a label the operating team may adjust at convenience.

### 2.2 The output name

**The output carries the feed's name.** The standard is explicit that *"a consumer should never need a lookup table to connect the two."* The output of `invoice-adjustments` is therefore named `invoice-adjustments` — not an abbreviation, not a separate internal identifier, not a table name unrelated to the feed name. This is the same rule that ties the landing-zone prefix (§3) to the feed.

### 2.3 If the feed is ever renamed

A rename is not a rename of a string; it runs through an **alias period**:

1. The old name keeps working while registered consumers move over.
2. The alias is retired **only when the delivery records show no reads against it** — not on a date chosen in advance, and not on the assumption that consumers have migrated.
3. Renaming without the alias period is *"treated as decommissioning one feed and launching another, with everything that obliges."*

"Registered consumers" is a defined population, not everyone who happens to read: see §5.4.

---

## 3. Where the output lands, and how that area is organized

The landing area is organized by **layout LZ-14**.

### 3.1 One prefix, named for the feed

Every feed owns **exactly one prefix, named for the feed**. `invoice-adjustments` therefore owns one prefix named `invoice-adjustments`, and everything the feed writes lands under it.

### 3.2 Partitioned by write date

Everything the feed writes under that prefix is **partitioned by write date**. This partitioning is not merely a convention for query performance — it is the unit of repair (§6) and the basis of the retention clock (§4.2), so it is load-bearing in two other standards.

### 3.3 The two write rules

- **Nothing writes outside its own prefix.** The layout states the consequence plainly: *"a feed that needs a second area is two feeds."* If `invoice-adjustments` turns out to need a second landing area — a side output, a reject stream, a differently-shaped extract — that is a second feed to be named and onboarded under FN-13 in its own right, not a second prefix for this one.
- **Nothing but the feed writes inside it.** The purpose of both rules together is that *"ownership of any object in the zone is readable from its path alone."*

### 3.4 What consumers may and may not do

Consumers **read from the prefix**. They do **not** write markers, checkpoints or scratch output into it. *Consumer state lives with the consumer.* This is worth stating to consuming teams at onboarding rather than discovering it later, because a consumer-written marker inside the prefix breaks the path-ownership property in §3.3.

---

## 4. Storage registration and how long the output lives

### 4.1 Register in exactly one tier

Every feed registers its output in **exactly one storage tier**, and *the tier decides the output's lifetime*. There is no per-feed retention setting to choose; choosing the tier is choosing the retention.

`invoice-adjustments` is a nightly operational feed, so it registers in **tier ST-16**, which is where nightly operational feeds go and where `parcel-events` itself sits. The Storage Tier Register states directly that *"a feed operated like it registers here too."*

### 4.2 Output lifetime: 47 days

Output in tier ST-16 is **purged 47 days after its write date.**

The clock runs from the write date, which is the same write date the output is partitioned by (§3.2) and the same write date a re-run must preserve (§6.2). A partition repaired by a re-run days later still carries the night it repairs as its identity, so a re-run does not extend that partition's life.

### 4.3 Keeping anything longer

Keeping output beyond 47 days is **not a setting the feed team may change**. It is a **re-registration into a retention tier**, and it is *"reviewed by the register's owners rather than granted by the feed team."* If any consumer of `invoice-adjustments` has a requirement to read output older than 47 days, that requirement must be taken to the register's owners as a re-registration before the feed goes live — it cannot be satisfied by the operating team after the fact.

### 4.4 Capacity: the registration is the draw

Registration is also where capacity is accounted for. Platform storage is bought ahead under a standing vendor commitment, so **a new registration draws against the Procurement Commitment Ledger** maintained by the procurement office. Registering the feed *is what makes the draw visible to them* — there is no separate capacity ticket that does this.

On the ledger side, the relevant commitment is **line PV-25**, the standing commitment for bulk storage:

- Draw-downs are recorded as internal registrations are made, and **the office sizes the renewal from the recorded draws** — *"an unrecorded draw is capacity the renewal will not cover."*
- **New draws are confirmed with the vendor manager before they begin.** Standing up `invoice-adjustments` is a new draw, so this confirmation is part of onboarding, not a follow-up.
- A draw that would take line PV-25 past its committed volume **waits for the renewal** rather than assuming headroom.
- Renewals run on the procurement office's own negotiation calendar. Teams planning a **large** draw are to talk to the office **a cycle ahead**.

Whether the expected nightly volume of `invoice-adjustments` counts as a "large" draw, and whether PV-25 currently has headroom for it, are not determined by anything recorded here — see **Open items**. The action that is determined: the vendor-manager confirmation happens before the draw begins.

---

## 5. When the feed is expected to land, and what happens when it is repeatedly late

### 5.1 Declare the landing hour

Every nightly feed **declares its expected landing hour in table LH-18**, and *the declaration is what consumers schedule against.* The standard's framing is blunt about the cost of skipping this: *"an undeclared feed has no lateness, only unpredictability."*

`invoice-adjustments` must therefore have an LH-18 declaration before it is treated as operating. **The specific hour to declare is not determined by anything recorded on the platform** — the declared hour for `parcel-events` is not in the material available here, and in any case the hour belongs to this feed's own upstream timing, not to `parcel-events`. It must be set by the owning team as part of onboarding. See **Open items**.

### 5.2 What "late" means

A feed landing **after its declared hour is late**. Lateness is tracked **per morning against the declaration** — the unit is the morning, not the run, and the reference is always the declared hour, never the feed's recent typical behaviour.

### 5.3 The escalation

- **One late morning is noted.** No escalation.
- **Repeated late mornings in the same week are raised with the owning team as a delivery matter.** The week is the window; repetition inside it is the trigger.
- The raised matter resolves one of exactly two ways: **either the window moves and the declaration is corrected, or the cause is fixed.** Continuing to run late against an unchanged declaration is not one of the outcomes.

### 5.4 Moving the window is a consumer-facing change

The standard closes off the obvious shortcut: *"Quietly re-declaring a later hour to absorb lateness is a change consumers must be told about like any other."* Correcting the LH-18 declaration therefore carries the announcement obligation, and announcements are not issued by the feed team in their own channel:

- A change is announced as an **AN-5 bulletin**, issued centrally *"so no consumer's notice depends on which team is making the change."*
- The bulletin is delivered to **every consumer the stream's agreement ledger lists**, and is **posted against the stream's register entry**. Where a delivered copy and the register disagree, **the register entry is authoritative.**
- Issued bulletins are corporate correspondence. Their retention is **not the announcing team's decision**: they are filed under the corporate records schedule. Under that directory, bulletins fall in **series RR-21**, are **filed with their delivery evidence at the time of issue** — *"filing is part of issuing, not an afterthought"* — and disposal is reviewed by the records office, not by the issuing team.

**Who counts as a consumer.** The Consumer Agreement Ledger defines the notice boundary. Each consuming team registers a **CA-9 agreement per stream it reads**, naming the consuming service, its owner, and the fields it depends on. Registration is *a condition of read access*, and it is also the notice boundary: *"a team that never registered is owed nothing, however long it has been reading."* Part of onboarding `invoice-adjustments` is therefore getting its intended consumers to register CA-9 agreements — an unregistered consumer has neither standing to be notified nor, strictly, read access.

When a stream's shape changes, agreements are reviewed, and *a consumer whose declared fields are untouched by a change may be notified without being waited for, at the announcing owner's discretion.*

### 5.5 A note on scope

The Change Announcement Directory describes the AN-5 bulletin as the mechanism for a **governed-stream** change. Whether `invoice-adjustments` is a governed-tier stream is not determined by anything recorded — see §8 and **Open items**. The declaration-correction obligation in §5.4 comes from the Delivery Expectation Standard, which applies to *every nightly feed* regardless; the governed-tier question affects only which additional obligations in §8 attach.

---

## 6. Re-running after a bad night

### 6.1 Replacement, not appending

**A re-run repairs a bad night by replacing it, never by appending to it.** This is the whole of **procedure RP-22** in one line, and it is the sentence to hold onto during an incident.

### 6.2 The mechanics

- The **affected write-date partitions are replaced whole**, under the feed's own prefix (§3.1). Partial patching of a partition is not the procedure.
- **The original write date stays the partition's identity.** A re-run performed days later **still lands under the night it repairs**, so *"consumers re-reading the partition see the corrected records where the bad ones were."*
- A re-run that would change a partition's write date **is not a re-run**: the procedure calls it *"a new feed writing into an old feed's zone, and the layout forbids it"* (§3.3). This is the single most important failure mode to avoid, because a re-run stamped with today's date looks superficially successful while silently leaving the bad night in place and violating LZ-14 at the same time.
- Because the write date is preserved, the ST-16 purge clock (§4.2) is unaffected by a re-run: the repaired partition is still purged 47 days after the *original* write date, which bounds how late a repair can usefully be made.

### 6.3 Order of operations relative to upstream

**Re-runs happen after the upstream collectors have drained for the affected window.** *"Re-running ahead of the upstream repair reproduces the bad night."*

This connects to the one substantive operating fact the Parcel Events Feed Runbook keeps for itself: `parcel-events` *"runs only after the parcel collectors drain,"* and consequently *"a missing hour in the output is a collector matter, not a feed matter, and re-running the feed cannot supply records a collector never delivered."*

The same shape of dependency should be expected to apply to `invoice-adjustments` — a nightly feed run after its upstream drains, with missing input being an upstream matter that no re-run can manufacture. **What the upstream of `invoice-adjustments` actually is, and what "drained" means for it, is not recorded anywhere on the platform.** It must be identified and written into this feed's own runbook before the feed is operated, because it is the precondition on both the nightly run and every re-run. See **Open items**.

### 6.4 What a re-run is not

A re-run is a repair of records under an unchanged contract. It does not change the feed's name (§2), its prefix (§3), its tier (§4), or its declared landing hour (§5). If a bad night is being "repaired" by writing a different record shape, that is a change to what the stream carries, not a re-run, and it is governed by §8 rather than by RP-22.

---

## 7. If any output is ever copied outside the platform

### 7.1 The standing rule

**No feed output leaves the platform on an operator's judgment alone.** This applies to any copy of `invoice-adjustments` output outside the platform, however small, however routine, and however internal the requesting party feels.

### 7.2 The EG-24 approval

Every copy outside the platform carries an **EG-24 approval** naming three things:

1. the **receiving party**,
2. the **purpose**, and
3. the **date the copy will be deleted**.

*"An approval without all three is returned unactioned."* There is no partial approval and no "deletion date to follow."

The approval is **filed before the copy is made**.

### 7.3 Re-copies

Re-copies under an existing approval are re-copies **only while the purpose and recipient are unchanged.** A new recipient, or the same recipient for a different purpose, is a new approval — not a continuation of the old one.

### 7.4 The covering instrument

An EG-24 approval **also cites the agreement that makes the transfer lawful.** The covering instrument is looked up in the **Data Sharing Agreement Register**, maintained by the legal office. *"A transfer with no instrument to cite does not proceed, whatever its purpose."*

On the register side:

- Each instrument is an **SA-27 entry** recording the **counterparty**, the **categories of records covered**, the **permitted purposes**, and the **instrument's expiry**.
- A transfer cites the SA-27 entry that covers it, and **the citation is checked against the entry's categories and purposes, not against the transferring team's intent.** A transfer that feels within spirit but falls outside the recorded categories is not covered.
- **An expired or absent instrument means the transfer waits for the legal office**, *"however routine the request."*
- The register is **the only authoritative list.** Copies of instruments held by teams are working copies, and **the register's expiry dates govern.** A team's own copy showing an instrument as live does not make it live.

### 7.5 Practical consequence for this feed

Because invoice adjustment records may plausibly be requested by outside parties (auditors, counterparties, vendors), the operating team should expect EG-24 requests and should treat the SA-27 lookup as the gating step, not the last formality. **Whether any SA-27 instrument today covers the record categories `invoice-adjustments` will carry is not determined by anything recorded here** — the register's contents are held by the legal office. See **Open items**.

---

## 8. Additional obligations if `invoice-adjustments` is classified as a governed-tier stream

This section applies **only if** `invoice-adjustments` is classified governed-tier. The Parcel Events Feed Runbook does not state whether `parcel-events` is governed-tier, and no classification for `invoice-adjustments` is recorded. It is included here because the classification question must be answered before go-live, and because the answer materially changes what a schema change costs. **Do not apply this section until the classification is confirmed** (see **Open items**).

A governed-tier stream *"feeds the statutory accounts, so its obligations are stricter than ordinary operational care."* If the classification applies:

- **Change classification.** Every change to what the stream carries is **classified before any work begins**, and **the owner cannot waive a classification**. An incompatible change to the record shape — *a field added, renamed, retyped or removed* — is **class RB-7**, which owes consumers **17 business days of advance notice** counted in the *consuming* teams' working calendar. The notice runs from the day the announcement is **actually delivered**. The class does not shorten for changes the producer considers small: *"compatibility is judged from the consumer's side."* Compatible additions and operational-only changes carry lighter classes that owe an announcement but no waiting period. **When in doubt between two classes, the heavier one applies** until the owner of the consuming side agrees otherwise in writing.
- **Schema version registration.** A new record-shape version is **registered before any producer writes it** — *"a record shape that reaches the stream unregistered is an incident, not a shortcut."* Each stream declares a compatibility mode in the register and every proposed version is checked against it at registration. (The strictest mode, **CM-3**, requires a new version to be readable by every consumer of the previous one without a code change; the register records the orders and settlement streams in that mode. Which mode `invoice-adjustments` would declare is not recorded.)
- **Attestation.** After a change lands, the producing service's owner files **form AT-12**, once the change is live and the first full settlement has passed, stating that the flowing records match the registered version, that no consumer-visible field was dropped, and that the announced scope is the delivered scope. The signature is **personal to the named service owner and cannot be delegated**; a vacancy in that role **suspends changes** rather than the attestation. An unattested change *"stays open in the tier's books and is raised at every review until the form is filed."*
- **Timing.** Change timing does not belong to the producing team alone: work on systems feeding the statutory accounts also observes the **company close calendar**, whose windows are set by the finance organization, not by engineering.

---

## 9. Onboarding checklist

| # | Step | Governing rule | Determined here? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Confirm the feed name `invoice-adjustments` as subject-then-grain | FN-13 | Yes — well-formed |
| 2 | Name the output identically to the feed | FN-13 | Yes |
| 3 | Create exactly one landing prefix named `invoice-adjustments`, partitioned by write date | LZ-14 | Yes (rule); physical root not recorded |
| 4 | Confirm no second output area is needed (if it is, that is a second feed) | LZ-14 | Yes |
| 5 | Register output in tier ST-16 | ST-16 | Yes |
| 6 | Confirm no consumer needs output older than 47 days; if so, raise re-registration with the register's owners **before** go-live | ST-16 | Requires consumer input |
| 7 | Confirm the new draw against line PV-25 with the vendor manager before it begins; flag early if large | PV-25 | Volume not recorded |
| 8 | Declare the expected landing hour in table LH-18 | LH-18 | **Hour not determined** |
| 9 | Get intended consumers to register CA-9 agreements (condition of read access and the notice boundary) | CA-9 | Consumers not recorded |
| 10 | Identify and document the upstream whose draining gates the nightly run and every re-run | RP-22 / runbook | **Not recorded** |
| 11 | Confirm governed-tier classification, and if it applies, register the schema version before first write | §8 | **Not determined** |
| 12 | Brief the operating team that any off-platform copy needs a filed EG-24 approval citing a live SA-27 instrument | EG-24 / SA-27 | Yes |
| 13 | Write this feed's own runbook, keeping only what is specific to it and pointing at the six standards for the rest | Parcel Events Feed Runbook, as model | Yes |

---

## Open items

The following are things this document needs and could not determine from what the platform records. None of them are invented below; each is listed as unresolved.

1. **The owning team for `invoice-adjustments`.** No owner is recorded. The Delivery Expectation Standard escalates repeated lateness "with the owning team," and (if §8 applies) the AT-12 attestation is personal to the named service owner — both require a named owner. The Parcel Events Feed Runbook does not name an owner for `parcel-events` either, so it cannot be inherited by analogy.

2. **The expected landing hour to declare in table LH-18.** Neither the hour for `invoice-adjustments` nor the declared hour for `parcel-events` is recorded on the platform. The declaration is mandatory before the feed can be said to have a lateness standard at all.

3. **The upstream that must drain before the nightly run and before any re-run.** `parcel-events` depends on "the parcel collectors"; the equivalent upstream for `invoice-adjustments` is not recorded. Both the nightly schedule and RP-22 re-runs are gated on it, and without it there is no way to distinguish "feed problem" from "upstream never delivered."

4. **What the feed writes — the record shape and content of an invoice adjustment record.** Nothing about the payload, fields, or grain semantics is recorded. This is needed for CA-9 consumer agreements (which name the fields a consumer depends on) and, if §8 applies, for schema version registration.

5. **Whether `invoice-adjustments` is a governed-tier stream.** Not recorded, and not derivable from the `parcel-events` material, which is silent on `parcel-events`' own tier. This determines whether §8 (RB-7 classification, 17-business-day notice, schema version register, AT-12 attestation, close-calendar timing) applies at all. Given the subject matter, this should be confirmed with the finance organization rather than assumed either way.

6. **If governed-tier: the compatibility mode `invoice-adjustments` declares in the Schema Version Register.** The register records the orders and settlement streams in mode CM-3; what mode this feed would declare is not recorded.

7. **The physical root of the landing area.** LZ-14 specifies the *organization* (one prefix per feed, named for the feed, partitioned by write date) but the concrete storage location or bucket the landing zone sits in is not recorded, and the platform reports no configured connections.

8. **Expected nightly volume, and whether line PV-25 has headroom for it.** The Procurement Commitment Ledger requires new draws to be confirmed with the vendor manager, requires large draws to be raised a cycle ahead of renewal, and makes a draw that would exceed the committed volume wait for renewal. Neither the expected volume nor PV-25's current position is recorded.

9. **The intended consumers of `invoice-adjustments`.** None are recorded. Consumers must register CA-9 agreements — this is both the read-access condition and the notice boundary — and their retention needs determine whether the 47-day ST-16 lifetime is sufficient (checklist item 6).

10. **Whether any SA-27 instrument covers the record categories this feed will carry.** The Data Sharing Agreement Register is held by the legal office and its contents are not visible here. This is only needed if and when an off-platform copy is requested, but a request will stall on it.

11. **The retention period for RR-21 bulletins.** The Corporate Records Retention Directory states that items in the series are kept "for the period the directory lists for the series"; the period itself is not reproduced in the available material. This is the records office's to state, not the feed team's.

# Change Plan — Adding a Field to `orders-ledger` Records

**Stream:** orders-ledger (governed tier)
**Change type:** addition of one new field to the record shape
**Plan date:** 2026-08-10
**Executing role:** the stream's owning team, under the personal signature of the producing service's named owner

---

## 1. What this change is, under the rules that apply to it

The orders-ledger stream carries the order lifecycle records every revenue report is built from, and its records feed the statutory accounts. It is a **governed-tier** stream, which means how it changes is bound by the tier obligations register rather than by the producing team's own judgment (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*; *Governed Tier Obligations*).

Three fixed determinations follow, and none of them are the owner's to vary:

| Determination | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Change class | **RB-7** — a field *added* to a stream's record shape is an incompatible record-shape change | Change Class Directory |
| Notice owed to consumers | **17 business days** before the change is applied, in the consuming teams' working calendar, running from the day the announcement is actually delivered | Change Class Directory |
| Compatibility mode of the registered schema | **CM-3**, the strictest — a new version must be readable by every consumer of the previous one without a code change | Schema Version Register |

Two constraints that owners commonly try to work around are closed explicitly by the material:

- **RB-7 does not shorten for changes the producer considers small.** Compatibility is judged from the consumer's side, not the producer's. A purely additive field is still RB-7.
- **The owner cannot waive a classification** (*Governed Tier Obligations*). Where two classes are arguable, the heavier one applies until the owner of the consuming side agrees otherwise in writing.

Note the interaction the owner must resolve before proposing: RB-7 treats a field addition as *incompatible*, while CM-3 requires the new version to be readable by every current consumer *without a code change*. These are two separate gates applied by two different bodies of rule — the class decides the notice owed, the compatibility mode decides whether the version may be registered at all. A new field that any current consumer cannot read without changing code fails CM-3 and cannot be registered as proposed, regardless of how much notice is given.

---

## 2. Sequence of execution

Steps are given in the order the rules require. Ordering constraints that are load-bearing are called out at each step.

### Step 1 — Classify the change before any work begins

**Who:** the stream's owning team.
**Rule:** every change to what a governed stream carries is classified *before any work begins* (*Governed Tier Obligations*). This precedes design, code, and proposal.

Record the classification as **RB-7**. Classification is what unlocks the rest of the sequence and fixes the 17-business-day obligation; it is not a formality performed alongside the work.

**Output:** a recorded RB-7 classification, which will later be carried on the schema register entry.

### Step 2 — Raise the proposal against the registered schema

**Who:** the stream's owning team.
**Rule:** any change to the record shape "starts with a proposal against the stream's registered schema" (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*).

The proposal should carry, at minimum, what the downstream gates will need to consume:

- the new field: name, type, nullability, semantics, and how it is populated;
- the proposed new schema version;
- the RB-7 classification from Step 1;
- the CM-3 compatibility argument — specifically, evidence that every current registered consumer of the *previous* version can read the new version **without a code change**;
- the intended apply date, and its standing against the close calendar (Step 6).

### Step 3 — Review the consumer agreement ledger and determine the notice list

**Who:** the stream's owning team, against the ledger.
**Rule:** each consuming team registers a **CA-9** agreement per stream it reads, naming the consuming service, its owner, and the fields it depends on. Registration is a condition of read access **and the notice boundary**: announcements are delivered to registered consumers, and a team that never registered is owed nothing, however long it has been reading (*Consumer Agreement Ledger*).

Do three things here:

1. **Pull the full CA-9 list for orders-ledger.** That list — not any informal list of known readers — is the delivery list for the bulletin and the population the 17 days is owed to.
2. **Review the agreements, as the ledger requires when a stream's shape changes.** For each registered consumer, note the fields it has declared a dependency on.
3. **Decide, per consumer, whether it must be waited for.** The ledger permits a consumer whose declared fields are untouched by a change to be *notified without being waited for*, at the announcing owner's discretion. A newly added field appears in no existing CA-9 declared-field list, so on its face this discretion is available for every consumer. It sits in direct tension with RB-7's rule that the class does not shorten and that compatibility is judged from the consumer's side. **The available material does not resolve which governs.** The conservative execution — and the one consistent with "when in doubt between two classes, the heavier one applies" — is to serve the full 17 business days to every registered consumer, and to shorten only for a consumer whose consuming-side owner has agreed otherwise **in writing**. If the owner instead exercises ledger discretion, that decision should be recorded per consumer, with reasons, alongside the proposal.

**Output:** the delivery list; the per-consumer wait/no-wait determination with its written basis; any written consuming-side owner agreements.

### Step 4 — Register the new schema version

**Who:** the stream's owning team, through the schema version register.
**Rule:** a new version is registered **before any producer writes it** — a record shape that reaches the stream unregistered is *an incident, not a shortcut* (*Schema Version Register*).

At registration, the proposed version is checked against orders-ledger's declared compatibility mode, **CM-3**: readable by every consumer of the previous version without a code change. This check happens at registration time and is the gate the change can actually fail.

The register entry is the authoritative answer to "what changed and when" and carries **the version, the classification of the change that produced it, and who approved it**. Ensure the RB-7 classification from Step 1 is carried onto the entry.

**Ordering:** registration must complete before any producer emits the new shape (Step 8). It does not itself authorise the apply — the notice period and the close-calendar check still stand between registration and go-live.

**If CM-3 fails:** the version cannot be registered as proposed. The change must be reshaped until every current consumer can read it without a code change, or the affected consuming-side owners must be brought into a written agreement before the version is put forward again. There is no registration-level waiver in the available material.

### Step 5 — Issue the AN-5 bulletin and start the notice clock

**Who:** *not the producing team.* Consumer-facing notices are issued **centrally**, so that no consumer's notice depends on which team is making the change (*Change Announcement Directory*). The owning team requests the bulletin; the central announcement function issues it.
**Rule:** a governed-stream change is announced as an **AN-5 bulletin**.

The bulletin is:

- **delivered to every consumer the stream's CA-9 agreement ledger lists** (the Step 3 list); and
- **posted against the stream's register entry**, which is the authoritative copy when a delivered copy and the register disagree.

The bulletin must state the delivered scope accurately, because the closing attestation will assert that *the announced scope is the delivered scope* (Step 9). Any change of scope after issue must therefore be re-announced, not absorbed.

**The clock:** the 17 business days runs **from the day the announcement is actually delivered** — not from the day it was drafted, approved, or posted — and is counted in the **consuming teams' working calendar**.

**Filing is part of issuing:** issued bulletins are corporate correspondence under **series RR-21** of the corporate records retention directory — formal correspondence the firm sends out in its own name and must be able to produce later. Items in the series are **filed with their delivery evidence at the time of issue**; filing is part of issuing, not an afterthought. Retention runs for the period the directory lists for RR-21, and disposal is reviewed by the records office, not by the issuing or announcing team.

Capture and file the **delivery evidence** at issue. It is both a records obligation and the only defensible proof of when the 17-day clock started.

### Step 6 — Check the apply date against the close calendar

**Who:** the stream's owning team, against the close calendar published by the financial control group.
**Rule:** change timing does not belong to the producing team alone — work on systems that feed the statutory accounts observes the **company close calendar**, whose windows are set by the finance organization, not by engineering (*Governed Tier Obligations*).

The binding window is **QW-4**, the quiet window running from **journal cutoff to statement sign-off**. During QW-4, systems whose figures flow into the statements are left as they are: **production alterations to those systems wait until the books are signed**, because an alteration mid-close turns every reconciliation difference into a question about the alteration. orders-ledger feeds the statutory accounts, so it is in scope.

Practical consequences for scheduling:

- The 17-business-day notice period may **run** across QW-4; what QW-4 prohibits is the **apply**.
- The apply date must fall outside QW-4 — after statement sign-off, or before journal cutoff with enough margin that the change and its first full settlement (Step 9) complete before cutoff.
- Period dates, cutoff times, and the current window's standing are published on the finance group's internal page **each period**. Confirm against the current period's publication; do not schedule from a remembered cadence.
- **Exception route, if one is genuinely needed:** the controller's office grants exceptions **in writing**, and treats them as **findings in the close report**. An exception is available but is not free — it lands as a finding.

### Step 7 — Hold until both gates are open

The change may be applied only when **both** of the following are true:

1. The 17 business days of RB-7 notice have elapsed for every consumer owed them (per the Step 3 determination), counted in the consuming teams' working calendar from actual delivery; **and**
2. The apply date is outside QW-4, or a written controller's-office exception is in hand.

Neither gate substitutes for the other, and the earlier gate does not start the later one.

### Step 8 — Apply the change

**Who:** the stream's owning team.

The producer begins writing the new record shape only after the version is registered (Step 4) and both gates are open (Step 7). A shape reaching the stream ahead of its registration is an incident.

The delivered scope must match the announced scope exactly. If it cannot, the correct action is to stop and re-announce rather than to deliver a different scope and reconcile it at attestation.

The stream settles during the **overnight window**, and its lag is reviewed each morning (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*). Plan the apply so the first settlement after it falls inside the normal overnight window, and use the morning lag review as the first observation of the change in production.

**Who:** the producing service's **named owner**, personally.
**Rule:** after any change lands, the owner re-attests the stream's completeness (*Governed Tier Obligations*; *Attestation Procedure*).

- **Form:** **AT-12**.
- **When:** once the change is **live and the first full settlement has passed** — not at deploy.
- **What it states:** that the records now flowing **match the registered version**; that **no consumer-visible field was dropped** along the way; and that the **announced scope is the delivered scope**.

- **If not filed:** an unattested change is treated as **unfinished however long it has been live**, stays open in the tier's books, and is **raised at every review** until the form is filed.

Unregistered readers are owed **nothing**, however long they have been reading. If the owning team knows of readers with no CA-9, the correct remedy is to get them registered, not to notify them off-ledger — but that is outside this change and confers no notice entitlement within it.

## 4. Constraints on *when* the change may be applied — consolidated

# Incident Handling Document — settlement-recon: Three Consecutive Failed Nights

**Control:** nightly settlement-recon job
**Trigger:** third consecutive failed nightly pass
**Audience:** the on-shift engineer who holds the job at the moment the third failure is observed
**Date prepared:** 2026-08-10

---

## 1. What has happened, in the platform's terms

The settlement-recon job agrees each day's settlement records against the processor statements. A clean pass is silent. A failed pass leaves that day **unagreed**, and the job re-attempts it the following night after the upstream statements refresh.

The recorded escalation ladder for failed nights is:

| Consecutive failed nights | What it is |
|---|---|
| 1 | Watched. No record opened. |
| 2 | Worked during the day. Still operational. |
| 3 | **No longer an operational matter.** An incident record is opened. |

Three consecutive failures have now occurred. The reason the third night is the threshold is stated explicitly in the runbook: the unagreed days now **span a statement cycle**. That fact is not incidental — it is the same fact that sets the severity band in §2, so record it plainly in the incident.

The job **keeps running on its normal schedule** for the whole life of the incident. Do not disable it, and do not suspend it to "stop the noise." A quiet night with the control disabled is explicitly disqualifying evidence for closure (see §6).

---

## 2. What is opened, and at what severity

### 2.1 The record

Open an **IN-28 incident record**. This is the record type the runbook names for a third consecutive failed night of settlement-recon.

The runbook is deliberate about the limit of the opening engineer's authority: *"The runbook's own scope ends at opening the record honestly."* Open it, describe the failure accurately, and then let the standards drive. Do not soften the description, and do not pre-judge the cause in the record.

### 2.2 Severity — this is not yours to choose

Severity is assigned **when the record is opened**, and it belongs to the Incident Severity Standard, not to the team that opened it or to the job's operators.

**This situation is band SB-8.** The standard's rule: *a reconciliation or settlement control failing across a statement cycle is band SB-8.* Settlement-recon is a settlement control, and three consecutive unagreed days span a statement cycle. The band follows from the facts; it is not a judgment call, and it must not be talked down to a lighter band because the failure is "just a job."

For contrast, the lighter bands cover **single-night failures and non-control degradations**. Those notify the owning team only and **do not escalate unattended**. Neither description fits here.

Everything downstream — who is notified, which escalation route runs, what the clocks are — is decided by SB-8, not renegotiated per incident.

---

## 3. Who has to be told, at opening

### 3.1 Notified by the severity band itself

Band SB-8 notifies, **at opening**:

1. **The owning team** for the settlement-recon job.
2. **The platform group's shift lead.**

Both notifications go out at the moment the record is opened — not after triage, not after a first look. The shift lead is also the first rung of the escalation route (§4), so this notification and the start of the escalation clock are the same event.

> The platform material does not record which named team owns settlement-recon, nor the individuals currently holding these roles. Resolve both from the current duty roster before sending; carried to **Open items**.

### 3.2 The compliance obligation that is not the engineering organization's to schedule

The Incident Severity Standard carries one further obligation for bands touching settlement controls, and it is explicit that this one is **not the engineering organization's to schedule**:

> When the failure falls inside a **statutory filing window**, notification follows the **Regulatory Filing Calendar** maintained by the compliance office.

What the calendar records, and why this is time-critical:

- The compliance office publishes statutory filing windows **a year ahead**. Each window names its filing, the lodgment date, and the **list of in-scope arrangements** the filing draws on.
- Where anything on that in-scope list **was interrupted while the filing was being prepared**, the office lodges **form RN-26** with the filing **before the window closes**, stating what was interrupted, the days affected, and the basis on which the filed figures stand.
- The office **can only lodge what it has been told while the window is open**. Word arriving after lodgment becomes a **correction**, which the regulators treat differently.

**What the on-shift engineer does with this:** as part of opening, check the published filing calendar for a window that is currently open and whose in-scope list includes the settlement arrangements this control agrees. If one is open, tell the compliance office **now**, in the same opening pass as §3.1 — not at closure, not in the review record. The compliance office confirms scope questions **in writing within a working day**, so if you cannot tell from the calendar whether the settlement arrangement is in scope, ask them in writing immediately rather than waiting. Note also that during a window the office's attention belongs to the filing rather than to new requests, which is a reason to send early, not a reason to hold off.

Include in that notification: the control affected, the three nights in question, and the fact that the days are unagreed. That maps directly onto what RN-26 needs.

> Whether a statutory filing window is open as of 2026-08-10, and whether settlement-recon's arrangements are on its in-scope list, is not determinable from the recorded material — the individual published windows are not in it. Carried to **Open items**.

---

## 4. How the escalation proceeds, and on what clocks

### 4.1 The route

Band SB-8 escalates along the **garnet route**. The division of authority is stated plainly: **severity decides the route, the roster decides the names, and the clock table decides the clocks.** A change to any one of the three does not edit the others.

The garnet route's rungs, **in order**:

| Rung | Role |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Platform shift lead** |
| 2 | **Duty manager** |
| 3 | **Head of platform operations** |

Two governing rules from the roster:

- An escalation **climbs one rung at a time and never skips a rung that has acknowledged.**
- An **escalation in flight finishes on the roster it started on.** If the roster is edited mid-incident, your escalation continues on the ladder it began with.

### 4.2 The clocks (settlement family of routes)

| Rung | Hold |
|---|---|
| Rung 1 — platform shift lead | **23 minutes** |
| Rung 2 — duty manager | **34 minutes** |
| Rung 3 — head of platform operations | **Holds until answered** — there is nowhere further to climb |

### 4.3 Rule AC-15 — what happens when nobody responds

Expiry is governed by **rule AC-15**:

- A clock that **runs out without an acknowledgment advances the call to the next rung on its own.** The engineer does not decide whether to escalate; expiry does it.
- The **missed rung is recorded as missed, and is not re-tried.** Do not loop back to a rung that timed out.
- **Acknowledging stops the climb at that rung.**
- **Declining passes it upward immediately, without waiting out the clock.**

### 4.4 The escalation as the on-shift engineer runs it

1. **T+0** — IN-28 opened; owning team and platform shift lead notified (§3.1); compliance notified if a window is open (§3.2). Rung-1 clock starts.
2. **T+0 to T+23min** — awaiting the shift lead.
   - Acknowledges → climb stops at rung 1. The shift lead now holds it.
   - Declines → advance to the duty manager **immediately**; do not wait out the remaining minutes.
   - Silence at **T+23min** → rung 1 is **recorded as missed**, not re-tried; the call advances to the duty manager and the 34-minute clock starts.
3. **T+23min to T+57min** — awaiting the duty manager. Same three outcomes: acknowledge stops the climb; decline advances immediately; silence at **T+57min** records rung 2 as missed and advances to the head of platform operations.
4. **From T+57min** — the head of platform operations **holds until answered**. There is no further rung and no further expiry. The call stays live on this rung; keep raising it until it is answered.

Record each acknowledgment, each decline, and each missed rung against the incident with its time as it happens. The missed-rung record is part of the incident's honest account of itself, and it feeds the timeline in §7.

---

## 5. What is communicated while the incident is open

Communications for a control-failure incident follow **cadence UC-11**. Its governing principle: *the cadence is a promise, and missing an update is itself reportable.*

### 5.1 The opening notice

The opening notice must name **all three** of:

1. **The affected control** — the nightly settlement-recon job.
2. **The days in question** — the three consecutive nights, and the settlement days left unagreed by them.
3. **When the next update will arrive.**

That third element sets the cadence for the rest of the incident. Choose an interval you can actually keep, because from that moment it is a promise you are measured against.

### 5.2 Updates while open

- Every update thereafter **either reports progress or re-promises the next time honestly.** "Nothing to report, next update at HH:MM" is a valid update; silence is not.
- **The audience never narrows.** Updates go to the **same audience as the opening notice**. Narrowing the audience mid-incident is **not permitted, however quiet the update** — a routine "no change" update goes to everyone the opening notice went to.
- Missing a promised update is itself a reportable event. If you will not make a promised time, send a re-promise before it passes, not an apology after.

### 5.3 The closing notice

The closing notice is part of the standard too. It goes to the **full audience**, and it **names the evidence the closure rests on** — i.e. it cites the CE-2 record described in §6.

> The recorded standard does not fix a numeric update interval for UC-11; it requires that the opening notice declare one and that every update honour or honestly re-promise it. It likewise does not enumerate the distribution list beyond the audience the opening notice sets — which, from §3, is at minimum the owning team and the platform shift lead, plus the compliance office where a filing window is open. Carried to **Open items**.

---

## 6. What has to be true before it can be closed

### 6.1 The standard

*A control-failure incident closes on evidence, not on silence.* Closure requires a **CE-2 evidence record**.

A CE-2 record is the control:

1. **Passing on its own schedule** — the record must come from **the scheduled run itself**;
2. **Unassisted**; and
3. **With the previously unagreed days brought current.**

All three conditions, together. Explicitly disqualifying:

- **A manually forced pass does not qualify.** A green result you triggered by hand is not a CE-2 record, no matter how correct its output.
- **A quiet night with the control disabled "qualifies even less."** Absence of failure is not evidence of a working control.

The CE-2 record is **attached to the incident before the closing notice goes out** — evidence first, then announcement, in that order.

### 6.2 Repairing the bad nights (what gets the days current)

Bringing the unagreed days current is repair work, and repair is governed by **procedure RP-22**:

- **A re-run repairs a bad night by replacing it, never by appending to it.** The affected **write-date partitions are replaced whole**, under the feed's own prefix.
- **The original write date stays the partition's identity.** A re-run performed days later still lands **under the night it repairs**, so consumers re-reading the partition see the corrected records where the bad ones were.
- A re-run that would change a partition's write date **is not a re-run** — it is a new feed writing into an old feed's zone, and the layout forbids it.
- **Re-run only after the upstream collectors have drained for the affected window.** Re-running ahead of the upstream repair **reproduces the bad night.** This matters especially here: the runbook already ties settlement-recon's nightly re-attempt to the upstream statements refreshing, so confirm the statements are in before repairing.

Note the ordering trap: a successful RP-22 repair is **not itself** the CE-2 record, because it is assisted. The repair brings the days current; the **next scheduled, unassisted, passing run** — with those days current — is the evidence. Plan for at least one clean scheduled night after the repair before closure is possible.

> RP-22 is written for a nightly *feed's* bad night and speaks in write-date partitions. The recorded material does not state whether settlement-recon writes partitioned output of that shape, so confirm the mapping with the owning team before repairing. Carried to **Open items**.

### 6.3 Closure checklist

- [ ] Upstream collectors drained for the affected window.
- [ ] Bad nights repaired under RP-22 — partitions replaced whole, original write dates preserved.
- [ ] A **scheduled** run has passed, **unassisted**, with the previously unagreed days **current**.
- [ ] **CE-2 record attached to the incident.**
- [ ] Closing notice sent to the **full audience**, **naming the CE-2 evidence**.
- [ ] Escalation history (acknowledgments, declines, missed rungs with times) recorded against the incident.
- [ ] If a filing window was open: the compliance office told **while the window was open**, so RN-26 could be lodged rather than a later correction.

---

## 7. What record it has to leave behind

Closing the incident does not discharge it. *"Once closed, the incident owes one more artifact."*

### 7.1 The PM-6 review record

Every closed control-failure incident files a **PM-6 review record**. It is due on the **Review Record Standard's own clock, not at closure time** — so closing the incident does not start it and does not excuse it.

The PM-6 record carries:

1. **A timeline of the nights in question** — the three failed nights, the repair, and the qualifying scheduled pass.
2. **The originating conditions as they are actually understood** — not a tidy narrative; what is genuinely known, with the unknowns left as unknowns.
3. **The corrections that will be made, with a named owner for each.**
4. **The review meeting's outcome.**

**Owned corrections are tracked to completion.** A record whose corrections have **no owner is returned to the incident's owner rather than filed.** An unowned correction is not a finding; it is an unfinished record.

### 7.2 Where it is filed

- **Against the incident**, and
- **Referenced from the control's own operating notes** — i.e. the Settlement Recon Job Runbook — *"so the next operator to meet the same failure finds what the last one learned."*

Both. Filing against the incident alone leaves the next on-shift engineer exactly where you started.

### 7.3 The people side — do this before the record is filed

The review record also closes the people side. **Hours spent on the nights in question are entered under the Worked Hours Ledger practice before the PM-6 record is filed**, because the workforce office's ledger closes on its own rhythm whether or not the review is done.

From the ledger practice:

- Ordinary working days flow in from **badge records** with no one's attention.
- **Hours worked outside the working day are different**: entered **by hand**, under code **TL-19**, with **the date and a one-line purpose**, **before the payroll cutoff of the following week.**
- **An unentered line lapses.** The ledger closes with payroll, and **a late claim reopens nothing.**
- Entered TL-19 hours accrue toward **time off in lieu**, at the rate the employment terms set; the balance shows beside leave in the workforce portal.
- A correction to a closed period is a **payroll correction**: applied by the payroll administrators on the following run, adjusting **pay**, never the closed ledger. Questions about a closed period go to the workforce office **in writing** and are answered against the ledger **as it closed**.

For a three-night settlement-recon incident, essentially all of the work is out-of-hours by definition — nightly job, night-shift response. **Enter TL-19 lines for every night worked, before next week's payroll cutoff.** This is the one deadline in this document that is genuinely unrecoverable: everything else can be repaired late, but a lapsed ledger line cannot.

> The TOIL accrual rate is set by the employment terms, which are not in the recorded material. Carried to **Open items**.

---

## 8. Sequence at a glance

| When | Action | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Third failure observed | Open **IN-28**; describe honestly | Settlement Recon Job Runbook |
| At opening | Severity is **SB-8** — not a local choice | Incident Severity Standard |
| At opening | Notify **owning team** + **platform shift lead** | Incident Severity Standard (SB-8) |

| T+23 min | Unacknowledged → rung 1 **recorded missed, not re-tried**; advance to duty manager, **34 min** | Rule AC-15 |
| T+57 min | Unacknowledged → rung 2 **recorded missed**; advance to head of platform operations, **holds until answered** | Rule AC-15 |

| Closing | Closing notice to full audience, **naming the CE-2 evidence** | Incident Communications Standard |

| On the standard's clock | **PM-6** review record filed against the incident **and** referenced from the runbook | Review Record Standard |
